Introduction 
Recent years have seen significant success in linguistic tasks, particularly machine translation, driven by the widespread adoption of neural models. However, domains such as medical and legal language present substantial challenges, often necessitating models trained on limited data. In these contexts, domain adaptation is crucial, yet obtaining high-quality training data remains difficult. Current neural models are highly effective but lack flexibility; adapting them to new domains typically demands accessing and processing substantial target-domain data for training. Alternatively, one could train separate models for each domain, which is inefficient and hampers knowledge sharing, especially when target data is scarce. Merely switching underlying corpora yields suboptimal results because models learn domain-specific linguistic patterns. A more effective strategy involves domain adaptation techniques, which have been extensively researched. These methods include mixing source and target data (requiring parallel data and a discriminator), employing domain embeddings (needing target data), and utilizing neural $N$-grams (also requiring target data). Despite these advancements, approaches facilitating easy domain adaptation with minimal or no target data remain limited.

In contrast to the inflexibility of current models, $N$-grams offer a viable alternative for low-resource domains, performing well where neural models struggle, as demonstrated in various studies. Moreover, $N$-grams are computationally efficient, scalable, and easily customizable by changing the training corpus. To leverage these advantages, we introduce a simple yet effective domain adaptation framework. K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. Furthermore, we introduce several new results concerning the embeddability of such spaces into Euclidean spaces and other Hilbertian environments. One significant finding is the establishment of a direct link between conformal embeddability and angle preservation when the target space is a Hilbertian space that supports a betweenness relation. Finally, we address a question raised by Godel and Turner in 1957 concerning the unique embeddability of betweenness-rich spaces into Hilbertian spaces that also possess an angle function.

To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable the remote monitoring of various damage types and mechanisms in structures, thereby facilitating advanced damage tolerance strategies and safety protocols for critical infrastructure.

Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, dense, large, or small. To facilitate widespread adoption, we developed an open-source implementation available at https://sourceforge.net/projects/nestedneumann/. Furthermore, we present detailed computational results from various iterative methods for matrix inversion using both synthetic and real-world datasets. These findings demonstrate that NN significantly outperforms NS, NI, and CI, with convergence speeds enhanced by a factor of over 200 for 2000x2000 matrices and over 1,000 for 50,000x50,000 matrices. The NN method's performance scales effectively with both matrix size and inception depth, provided the calculations remain feasible within available memory. These results indicate that NN is a highly effective iterative technique for computing approximate inverses of large matrices.
